title: Fewer wants
tomorrow: the Buddha gave Anuruddha an eighth thought. what was it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, fewer things: the forest monks' short list of what a life needs. Today, the harder part, the wanting underneath the things.

Somewhere tonight, someone is watching a video of a bright, empty apartment and adding a new set of storage boxes to a cart. Wanting less can quietly become one more thing to want. An old monk met the same knot. Anuruddha is sitting alone in a bamboo park, far from his teacher, and a thought arrives: this teaching is for one who wants little, not for one who wants much. Six more thoughts follow it, each one clear. And then, the sutta says, quick as a strong man bends his arm, the Buddha is standing in front of him.
screen: `THE EMPTY APARTMENT, THE FULL CART.` → `ANURUDDHA, ALONE.` → `THIS TEACHING IS FOR ONE WHO WANTS LITTLE.` → `THE BUDDHA ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Good, good, Anuruddha, he says. These are the thoughts of a great person. Then he unpacks the first one, few wants, and the unpacking has a twist. Someone of few wants, he says, doesn't even want people to know that they want little. Read that twice. You can want a smaller life and still be wanting something: to be seen as the simple one, the calm one, the one who needs nothing. The Buddha closes that door too. The Pali word is appicchatā, wanting little. Beside it in the sutta sits contentment: a monk content with whatever robe, whatever food, whatever shelter, whatever medicine comes. Not content with nothing. Content with enough. That's what makes this a Buddhist teaching and not a decluttering tip. In the first sermon, craving is named as the source of suffering. Fewer things clears a room. Fewer wants clears the mind that keeps filling rooms. So Buddhists practice it small: a monk eats what is put in the bowl, and on holy days some lay people keep extra precepts and go without a comfort or two. And Anuruddha? The sutta says he went back to his solitude, practiced, and became one of the awakened. But before he went, the Buddha handed him one more thought, an eighth, that he hadn't thought of.
screen: `GOOD, GOOD, ANURUDDHA.` · `DON'T EVEN WANT TO LOOK SIMPLE.` · `CONTENT WITH ENOUGH, NOT NOTHING.` · `FEWER WANTS CLEARS THE MIND.` · then, large: `FEW WANTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting this week: a pair of shoes, a reply, a bit of praise. Hold it in mind through the sit without buying, checking or deciding anything. Just notice the pull, where it sits in the body, and how it changes when nothing feeds it.
Fewer wants: appicchatā in Pali, wanting little, without even wanting to look like someone who wants little.
Pocket this one: few wants, and content with enough. Forty days into a life of practice.

chat.meaning: In AN 8.30 few wants is the first thought of a great person, paired with contentment: enough, not nothing.

notes: AN 8.30 paraphrased: Anuruddha, dwelling among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park, thinks seven thoughts (few wishes, contentment, seclusion, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom); the Buddha appears 'as a strong man would extend his arm', says 'good, good', adds the eighth (delight in non-proliferation), and explains each: one of few wishes does not wish others to know he is of few wishes. Anuruddha then becomes an arahant. Counts (seven, eighth) are the sutta's own.
The bamboo park is the sutta's Pacinavamsadaya; voiced simply as 'a bamboo park'. Confirm.
Holy-day practice framed as 'some lay people keep extra precepts' (AN 8.41); confirm.

Shape: story (Anuruddha alone, then the Buddha appears). Mai's two-week arc (days 1765–1778): Ông sells his house and moves in with Mai's family; the lessons follow the move, his new room, and the festival year. Days 1739–1764 were not on disk when written; the arc starts fresh here.
Surprising fact: the sutta says someone of few wants doesn't even want to be known for it.
